textbookText: Physiology of respiration In frog, entire process of respiration can be discussed under the following headings:

1. Breathing or external respiration: It is the process of taking in oxygen and throwing out carbon dioxide. As discussed earlier, this process occurs in frog through moist skin, buccopharyngeal cavity and lungs.

2. Transport of oxygen: A very few amounts of oxygen (about 1%- 3%) is dissolved in the blood plasma which is transported to different parts of the body. In RBC, an ironbased protein called haemoglobin is present. When haemoglobin combines with oxygen, an unstable compound called oxyhaemoglobin is formed. Most of the oxygen (about 97%- 99%) is transported by the blood in the form of oxyhaemoglobin to the tissues. One molecule of haemoglobin transports four molecule of oxygen. Formation of oxyhaemoglobin is favoured by decreased CO2 concentration, low temperature etc. in the blood.

3. Internal respiration: Oxyhaemoglobin is unstable compound which dissociates into oxygen and haemoglobin near the tissues because of some factors like more CO2 concentration, high temperature etc. Oxygen enters the body cell where glucose burns with oxygen to release energy, carbon dioxide and water.

4. Transport of CO2: CO2 is released in internal respiration as wastes which diffuse out from the cell to the blood. Then, it is transported to the lungs in the form of carbonic acid, bicarbonates and carbamino compound: i. In the form of carbonic acid (7%): Few amounts of carbondioxide is transported in the form of carbonic acid. Water in plasma combines with carbondioxide to form carbonic acid which is transported to the lungs for its expulsion. ii. In the form of bicarbonates (70%): Most of the carbondioxide produced is transported in the bicarbonate form. CO2 diffused to the blood combines with water in RBC to form carbonic acid in the presence of carbonic anhydrase. Carbonic acid ionises into H+ and HCO3‾‾. Then, majority of HCO3‾‾ shift into the plasma from RBC. To compensate the loss of HCO3‾‾, Cl‾‾ from plasma diffuses into RBC. This phenomenon is called chloride shift or Hamburger phenomenon. Now HCO3‾‾ in plasma combines with Na+ to form sodium bicarbonate and transported to lungs for the elimination of CO2.

iii. In the form of carbamino compound (23%): When carbondioxide reacts with haemoglobin it forms unstable carbamino compound (HbNHCOOH). It is transported to the lungs and gets dissociated to release carbondioxide for the expulsion.
